title: Use a Thin Trigger and a Focused Handler
summary: Validate the whole incoming collection while keeping business rules outside the trigger entry point.
prerequisites: Complete the earlier Junior lessons and use only your personal learning org.
learningObjectives: Choose a trigger event from the requirement.
Separate context dispatch from business rules.

sections.heading: Understand what starts a trigger
body: An Apex trigger runs in response to specified database events, such as inserting or updating records. Before triggers run before the final stored result is established and can be useful for checking or changing incoming values. After triggers serve different needs, including work that relies on saved identifiers. Choose the event from the requirement rather than using after update for every problem.

Oleg agrees two small rules for this lesson. A Confirmed appointment must identify its vehicle, customer, and scheduled time. An existing Completed appointment must not change status. This is not a complete scheduling state machine: it does not check calendar overlap or guarantee that every possible business transition is covered. Those limits are explicit.

callouts.text: A trigger is an entry point. The handler should express a small, named business responsibility.

sections.heading: Read old and new values for the whole collection
body: Trigger.new contains the incoming records for supported events. Trigger.oldMap provides previous records keyed by ID for update scenarios. Comparing old and new values lets the handler distinguish an actual transition from an unrelated edit. Repeating the same Completed status is not a change and should not be rejected by the terminal-status rule.

The handler loops over every incoming record, not only the first. addError marks an invalid record with an explanation. Whether a caller permits partial success affects the overall save result; the normal all-or-none DML statement can fail the group. Do not claim that addError always produces exactly the same batch outcome regardless of the calling operation.

The handler below performs no query or DML. It validates the pending records directly. That avoids an unnecessary update of the same records from inside their own update trigger, a common source of repeated execution. The class sharing declaration is not the mechanism enforcing these business rules; the explicit checks are.

callouts.text: Trigger execution context and database-operation defaults are version-sensitive. This API 68.0 example avoids database operations inside the handler.

sections.heading: Make the contract visible in tests
body: Create a valid Confirmed appointment with all three references or values. Then attempt to confirm an incomplete request and expect the explanatory failure. For the transition rule, create an appropriate synthetic Completed appointment and attempt to move it back to Requested. Also edit an unrelated allowed field while leaving Completed unchanged; this specific rule should not reject that operation.

Include multiple records in a single DML call so that the loop matters. A handler that only checks pending[0] could pass a single-record example while ignoring the rest. In J22, turn these cases into automated tests with assertions. For now, record the predicted and observed behaviour carefully.

If an equivalent validation rule already enforces the same condition from an earlier experiment, decide which implementation owns the rule. Avoid keeping two independent copies simply because both seem harmless. They can produce duplicate messages and drift when the requirement changes. Document the chosen implementation and any disabled experimental rule in the handover.

callouts.text: Include an invalid record after the first position in your batch. The first record alone is not a sufficient trigger test.

exercise.title: Submit a trigger with a narrow responsibility
exercise.brief: Implement and explain the two agreed validation rules.
steps: Keep the trigger limited to context dispatch.
Test valid insert, invalid confirmation, completed-status change, and unchanged completed status.
Repeat with a collection containing an invalid record beyond position zero.
acceptance: The handler contains no unnecessary self-update.
The submission states what the rules do not guarantee.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why use old values?
knowledgeCheck.answer: They distinguish a transition from an unrelated edit that keeps the same status.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why avoid updating the same records again in this handler?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The before-event records are already being saved, and another update can cause unnecessary recursion.

knowledgeCheck.question: Does this prevent double booking?
knowledgeCheck.answer: No. The rules check required confirmation information and a terminal status, not scheduling conflicts.

recap: Choose a trigger event from the requirement.
Separate context dispatch from business rules.
